C1.text: The actual split of chores explains only a small part of the variation in a partner's perceived fairness.
C1.reading: Weakly supported by single studies: the actual split plus controls explains about 5 to 19% of a partner's perceived fairness, though its slope is steep and partners at similar splits differ in perceived fairness.

C2.text: Comparison referents predict a partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C2.reading: Partly supported by one study (Italian survey): comparison referents predict perceived fairness net of a self-reported split for male referents, not for female ones, with possible self-serving bias; no review-level evidence.

C3.text: The justifications a partner accepts for an unequal split predict that partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C3.reading: No direct test in the nine papers read; one Swedish study is mixed (reduced employment is not accepted as a justification). Gager 1998 and Perales 2014 are requested.

C4.text: A partner's perceived fairness is more strongly associated with that partner's relationship satisfaction than the actual split is.
C4.reading: Open: three single studies disagree (the 30-country study favours perceived fairness over the split; the German panel and UK couple study do not) and none compares the two associations directly.

C5.text: The association between the actual split and relationship satisfaction is mediated by perceived fairness.
C5.reading: Not formally tested in any paper read; only a coefficient-change argument in one cross-sectional preprint, and two papers state that mediation is untested. Lavee & Katz 2002 (abstract only) claims it.

C6.text: Each partner over-claims their own contribution: the two partners' self-reported shares of chores sum to more than the whole.
C6.reading: Weak support from one UK couple study: the two partners' own shares of chores sum to 102 to 107% (largest for cognitive labour); an Italian survey shows no excess on average; unconfirmed by a matched-couple test.

C7.text: Which chores a partner does predicts that partner's perceived fairness beyond the time the chores take.
C7.reading: No direct test in the papers read: a Dutch study finds housework and childcare equally related to unfairness but cannot separate chore type from time; Carlson 2018 is requested.

C8.text: Studies measure perceived fairness of the division of chores mainly with a single self-report item.
C8.reading: Supported as a practice, not as a prevalence: 7 of the 8 papers read that measure perceived fairness use one self-report item, but no review of measures was read.

C9.text: A partner who is over-benefited by the allocation reports lower relationship satisfaction than a partner in an equitable allocation.
C9.reading: Contradicted for chores in one volunteer survey and supported for 'a bit less than fair share' in a German panel; no study contrasts over-benefit with an equitable allocation, so the claim stays open.
